entries.test: Whether any major cyber catastrophe attributed to Mythos (e.g. a Fortune 100 company brought down, large internet outages, a breach of defense systems) was publicly reported between April and June 2026.
entries.note: 'The world has not ended' is hyperbole. The normalisation reasonably reads it as saying the feared Mythos-driven catastrophe did not happen.

Marcus only points out the timing, sarcastically. The words 'which suggests the release was driven by business pressure' are the drafter's inference, and Anthropic's motive cannot be shown by public evidence.

entries.test: Reporting or survey data from around June 2026 showing whether companies had begun capping or cutting their AI token budgets after a period of heavy token use.
entries.note: 'Tokenmaxxing' is loose slang, but the second half (companies limiting token budgets) gives it a plain reading.

entries.test: Whether Anthropic made Mythos generally available, with added safeguards, by early June 2026.
entries.note: 'Widely' is supported by his next line: 'Anyone can now use it, for the right price.'
He hedges with 'probably', even though 'never in a million years' sounds emphatic.

entries.test: Anthropic's past public statements about not advancing the frontier, and whether it released a new frontier model around June 2026 that it promoted with benchmark-leading results.
entries.note: 'Hellbent on racing everyone' is rhetorical colour. The checkable core is the earlier statement and the new release.
'Played the media like a fiddle' is a figure of speech that implies deliberate manipulation. Neither the intent nor 'so many folks ate it up' has a shared test.

entries.test: Whether the GPT-2 (2019) and Mythos (2026) releases, along with any others by the same people, each followed a public 'too dangerous' warning, then media hype, then release.
entries.note: The word 'play' implies intent, which cannot be checked. The observable pattern of warnings followed by releases can be.
